### Model 1: Linear Persistence Models, Dim Evenings
```{r persistence-dim-with-s1}
pvt_persistence_dim <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_length_dim))

model_persistence_dim_numeric <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_length_dim + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_dim,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_dim_numeric)
```
```{r persistence-dim-no-s1}
pvt_persistence_dim_no_s1 <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_length_dim), exp_session > 1)

model_persistence_dim_no_s1 <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_length_dim + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_dim_no_s1,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_dim_no_s1)
```

Interpretation Exploratory 4 Persistence, Linear, Dim: To test whether consecutive dim light evenings produce cumulative effects on PVT performance, the linear relationship between run length (number of consecutive dim evenings) and PVT performance was examined. Two models were fitted, whilst the first model includes all observations, the second model excludes Session 1, as there is no controlled light exposure on the previous day, which might influence results. 

- Including Session 1 for dim evening analysis did not find a linear effect of consecutive dim evenings for PVT performance (β=-0.01194, p=0.845)

- Excluding Session 1 for dim evening analysis did not find a linear effect of consecutive dim evenings for PVT performance (β=-0.01692, p=0.763)

The negative (non-significant) coefficients suggest a slight decrease in mean response speed for consecutive dim light evening exposure, however this trend is not statistically significant. 

### Model 2: Linear Persistence Models, Bright Evenings
```{r persistence-bright-with-s1}
pvt_persistence_bright <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_length_bright))

model_persistence_bright_numeric <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_length_bright + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_bright,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_bright_numeric)
```
```{r persistence-bright-no-s1}
pvt_persistence_bright_no_s1 <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_length_bright), exp_session > 1)

model_persistence_bright_no_s1 <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_length_bright + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_bright_no_s1,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_bright_no_s1)
```

Interpretation Exploratory 4 Persistence, Linear, Bright: To test whether consecutive bright light evenings produce cumulative effects on PVT performance, the linear relationship between run length (number of consecutive dim evenings) and PVT performance was examined. As the first evening light exposure was dim for all participants, the analysis including and excluding session 1 are the same. 

A significant linear persistence effect was found for consecutive bright evenings (β=0.1400, p=0.0128), indicating that every additional evening bright light exposure improved mean response speed by around 0.14 resp./sec.


### Model 2: Categorical Persistence Models, Dim Evenings
```{r persistence-dim-categorical-with-s1}
pvt_persistence_dim <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_category_dim))

model_persistence_dim_categorical <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_category_dim + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_dim,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_dim_categorical)

anova(model_persistence_dim_numeric, model_persistence_dim_categorical)
```
```{r persistence-dim-categorical-no-s1}
pvt_persistence_dim_no_s1 <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_category_dim), exp_session > 1)

model_persistence_dim_categorical_no_s1 <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_category_dim + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_dim_no_s1,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_dim_categorical_no_s1)

anova(model_persistence_dim_no_s1, model_persistence_dim_categorical_no_s1)
```

Interpretation Exploratory 4 Persistence, Categorical, Dim:

In order to examine potential non-linear patterns of cumulative dim light exposure on mean response speed, a model was fitted using the categories second (2nd day cumulative dim light exposure) and third (3rd day cumulative dim light exposure)  compared to the first dim night (reference category) to predict PVT performance. As in the linear persistence analysis, two models (first with, second without first experimental session) were fitted. 

- Including Session 1 for dim evening analysis did not find non-linear effects of consecutive dim evenings for PVT performance: Second (β=0.02534, p=0.820), Third (β=-0.03895, p= 0.761).

- Excluding Session 1 for dim evening analysis did not find non-linear effects of consecutive dim evenings for PVT performance: Second (β=0.02252, p=0.824), Third (β=-0.04522, p= 0.693).

These results are in alignment with the dim, linear analysis, indicating neither linear nor non-linear effects of consecutive evening dim light exposure on PVT performance. 

### Model 2: Categorical Persistence Models, Bright Evenings
```{r persistence-bright-categorical-with-s1}
pvt_persistence_bright <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_category_bright))

model_persistence_bright_categorical <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_category_bright + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_bright,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_bright_categorical)

anova(model_persistence_bright_numeric, model_persistence_bright_categorical)
```
```{r persistence-bright-categorical-no-s1}
pvt_persistence_bright_no_s1 <- pvt_persistence %>% filter(!is.na(run_category_bright), exp_session > 1)

model_persistence_bright_categorical_no_s1 <- lmer(
  mean_response_speed ~ run_category_bright + (1 | participant_id),
  data = pvt_persistence_bright_no_s1,
  REML = FALSE
)

summary(model_persistence_bright_categorical_no_s1)

anova(model_persistence_bright_no_s1, model_persistence_bright_categorical_no_s1)
```

Interpretation Exploratory 4 Persistence, Categorical, Bright: In order to examine potential non-linear patterns of cumulative bright light exposure on mean response speed, a model was fitted using the categories second (2nd day cumulative bright light exposure) and third (3rd day cumulative bright light exposure)  compared to the first bright night (reference category) to predict PVT performance As the first evening light exposure was dim for all participants, the analysis including and excluding session 1 are the same. 

A significant effect of the third consecutive bright evening was found Third (β= 0.2733, p=0.018), whereas the second consecutive bright evening did not yield statistical significance (β= 0.1634, p= 0.146). 


### Interpretation Exploratory 4 Persistence Analysis 

**Dim Nights**: No evidence for persistence effects of cumulative dim nights with respect to PVT performance. Linear model including session 1 (β = -0.01, p = 0.91) and linear model without session 1 (β = -0.01, p = 0.86), showed no linear effect of run length of dim evenings of PVT performance. Also the categorical model showed no effects for analysis with session 1 (Second Night β = 0.04, p = 0.75; Third Night β = -0.03, p=0.81) nor analysis without session 1 (Second Night β = 0.04, p = 0.72; Third Night β = -0.03, p = 0.77). 

**Bright Nights**: Significant cumulative effects were observed. Each additional consecutive bright evening improved response speed by 0.14 responses / sec (β = 0.14, p = 0.01) within the linear model. Also the categorical model revealed significant findings for the third cumulative bright night (Second Night β = 0.16, p = 0.15; Third Night β = 0.27, p = 0.02). Comparing AIC values, the linear bright analysis revealed better fit (AIC: linear 46.0 vs categorical 47.9).

**Conclusion**: The exploratory persistence analysis revealed dose-dependent cumulative effects for bright light exposure. Multiple consecutive bright evenings produce progressively greater improvements in vigilance. These findings indicate that the temporal pattern of light exposure matters.

### Summary of Exploratory Analyses

The primary model (m1b_pvt: Light_Lag0_num + Light_Lag1_num) with random intercepts only was selected as the final primary model. Exploratory analyses examined model extensions:

* **Random slopes**: Adding random slopes for Light_Lag0 and/or Light_Lag1 did not improve model fit (ΔAIC: +3.2 for Lag0 slopes, +9.1 for both slopes) and produced singular fits, indicating insufficient between-participant variance to justify random slopes. 

* **Demographic moderation**: Testing sex and age interactions with Light_Lag0 and Light_Lag1 did not improve model fit (AIC: 63.7 vs 57.1 for primary model, ΔAIC = +6.6). No significant moderation effects emerged (all interaction p > 0.15), though the small sample (n=8) precludes definitive conclusions about individual differences.

* **Light lag interactions**: Testing 2-way interactions between Light_Lag0, Light_Lag1, and Light_Lag2 did not improve model fit (ΔAIC = +3.3). The Lag0 × Lag1 interaction showed a marginal trend (β = +0.224, p = 0.080), but the simpler additive model was preferred, supporting independent contributions of same-day and previous-day light exposure.

* **Persistence analysis**: Exploratory analysis (n=85 observations, 8 participants, sessions 1-13) tested whether consecutive exposure to the same light condition produces cumulative effects. For dim nights, no persistence effects were observed (linear model: β = -0.007, p = 0.91; categorical model ΔAIC = +1.8). For bright nights, significant cumulative benefits emerged: each additional consecutive bright evening improved response speed by 0.14 responses/sec (β = 0.140, p = 0.013, ~3% per night). The categorical model confirmed benefits were most pronounced by the third consecutive night (β = +0.273, p = 0.018), though the linear model provided better fit (ΔAIC = +1.9). These findings suggest sustained multi-day bright light schedules may be more effective than intermittent exposure, but remain hypothesis-generating given the small sample.

**Final model**: Model m1b_pvt (n=67, 8 participants, sessions 3-13) with fixed effects for Light_Lag0 and Light_Lag1, with random intercepts only.

### Model Comparison Overview
```{r model-comparison-table}
# Helper functions to extract coefficients from LMM
get_coef_lmm <- function(model, coef_name) {
  coefs <- summary(model)$coefficients
  if (coef_name %in% rownames(coefs)) {
    return(coefs[coef_name, "Estimate"])
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
}

get_p_lmm <- function(model, coef_name) {
  coefs <- summary(model)$coefficients
  if (coef_name %in% rownames(coefs)) {
    return(coefs[coef_name, "Pr(>|t|)"])
  } else {
    return(NA)
  }
}
```

Note:

Final Model Selection: m1b (row 3, highlighted in blue) was selected as the final model based on:

1. Superior fit compared to simpler models 

2. Both Lag 0 (β = 0.219, p = 0.001) and Lag 1 (β = 0.166, p = 0.013) significant

3. No improvement with additional complexity (m1c ΔAIC = +0.9; m2 ΔAIC = +1.3; m3 ΔAIC = +2.7)

4. Overall good / satisfied diagnostics (normality: Shapiro p = 0.89, homoscedasticity: Levene p = 0.22)

5. Parsimony (5 parameters, no multicollinearity: VIF = 1.0)

The hierarchical model building (rows 1-6) identified Lag 0 and Lag 1 as significant predictors. Adding Lag 2 (m1c), session effects (m2), or quadratic terms (m3) did not improve model fit.

All exploratory analyses (rows 7-14) tested model extensions. Random slopes models produced singular fits, indicating insufficient between-participant variance. Demographic moderation and light lag interactions did not improve fit. Persistence analysis revealed significant cumulative effects for bright nights only (β = +0.14 resp/sec per consecutive night, p = 0.013).

### Final Model: Fixed Effects
```{r final-model-effects}
# Extract fixed effects from m1b_pvt
m1b_coef <- summary(m1b_pvt)$coefficients

# Create results table with Benjamini-Hochberg correction
m1b_results <- data.frame(
  Effect = c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"),
  Beta = round(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "Estimate"], 3),
  SE = round(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "Std. Error"], 3),
  t = round(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "t value"], 3),
  p = format.pval(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "Pr(>|t|)"], 
                  digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  p_adj = format.pval(p.adjust(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "Pr(>|t|)"], 
                                method = "BH"), digits = 3, eps = 0.001),
  Effect_size = paste0("+", round(m1b_coef[c("Light_Lag0_num", "Light_Lag1_num"), "Estimate"], 2), 
                       " resp/sec")
)

kable(m1b_results, 
      col.names = c("Effect", "β (resp/sec)", "SE", "t", "p", "p (BH-adj)", "Effect Size")) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
```
```{r final-model-variance}
# Variance components for m1b_pvt
vc_final <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(m1b_pvt))

cat("\n**Variance Components (m1b_pvt):**\n")
cat("Between-participant (Random Intercept):", round(vc_final$vcov[1], 3), "\n")
cat("Within-participant (Residual):", round(vc_final$vcov[2], 3), "\n\n")

# Calculate ICC
icc_final <- vc_final$vcov[1] / (vc_final$vcov[1] + vc_final$vcov[2])
cat("ICC (Intraclass Correlation):", round(icc_final, 3), 
    paste0("(", round(icc_final * 100, 1), "% of variance between participants)"), "\n\n")

cat("**Model Fit:**\n")
cat("AIC:", round(AIC(m1b_pvt), 1), "| BIC:", round(BIC(m1b_pvt), 1), "\n")
cat("N obs:", nrow(pvt_lmm), "| N participants:", 
    length(unique(pvt_lmm$participant_id)), "\n")
cat("Family: Gaussian (identity link)\n\n")
```
```{r final-model-summary}
cat("**Primary Findings:**\n\n")

# Extract coefficients
beta_lag0 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag0_num", "Estimate"]
se_lag0 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag0_num", "Std. Error"]
t_lag0 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag0_num", "t value"]

beta_lag1 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag1_num", "Estimate"]
se_lag1 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag1_num", "Std. Error"]
t_lag1 <- m1b_coef["Light_Lag1_num", "t value"]

# Calculate 95% CI for Lag 0
ci_lower_lag0 <- beta_lag0 - 1.96 * se_lag0
ci_upper_lag0 <- beta_lag0 + 1.96 * se_lag0

# Calculate 95% CI for Lag 1
ci_lower_lag1 <- beta_lag1 - 1.96 * se_lag1
ci_upper_lag1 <- beta_lag1 + 1.96 * se_lag1

# Calculate baseline mean for percentage calculation
baseline_mean <- mean(pvt_lmm$mean_response_speed[pvt_lmm$Light_Lag0_num == 0 & pvt_lmm$Light_Lag1_num == 0], 
                      na.rm = TRUE)

# Lag 0 Effect
cat("**Same-Day Effect (Lag 0):**\n")
cat("Bright evening light (1000 lx) improves response speed by ", 
    round(beta_lag0, 2), " responses/sec\n", sep = "")
cat("(95% CI: [", round(ci_lower_lag0, 2), ", ", round(ci_upper_lag0, 2), 
    "]) compared to dim light (10 lx).\n", sep = "")
cat("This represents a ", round((beta_lag0 / baseline_mean) * 100, 1), 
    "% improvement relative to baseline.\n", sep = "")
cat("β = ", round(beta_lag0, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_lag0, 3), 
    ", t = ", round(t_lag0, 3), ", p = 0.001\n\n", sep = "")

# Lag 1 Effect
cat("**Previous-Day Effect (Lag 1):**\n")
cat("Bright light from the previous evening improves response speed by ", 
    round(beta_lag1, 2), " responses/sec\n", sep = "")
cat("(95% CI: [", round(ci_lower_lag1, 2), ", ", round(ci_upper_lag1, 2), "]).\n", sep = "")
cat("This represents a ", round((beta_lag1 / baseline_mean) * 100, 1), 
    "% improvement relative to baseline.\n", sep = "")
cat("β = ", round(beta_lag1, 3), ", SE = ", round(se_lag1, 3), 
    ", t = ", round(t_lag1, 3), ", p = 0.013\n\n", sep = "")

# Combined Effect
combined_effect <- beta_lag0 + beta_lag1
cat("**Combined Effect (Both Nights Bright):**\n")
cat("When both the current and previous evening have bright light exposure,\n")
cat("response speed improves by ", round(combined_effect, 2), " responses/sec\n", sep = "")
cat("(", round((combined_effect / baseline_mean) * 100, 1), "% improvement).\n", sep = "")
```
